opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

When people talk about foundation models for robotics, I think we first have to be honest about why robotics has been so hard for so long. In language, we had the internet: trillions of tokens, essentially free. In robotics, every piece of data comes from a physical machine interacting with the physical world. It's expensive, slow, and often unsafe to collect. So the core learning problem has always been data scarcity, and the core deployment problem has been generalization. A robot trained in one factory, one kitchen, or one lighting condition often fails the moment you move it somewhere else.

What's exciting about this new generation of foundation models is that they attack both problems at once. On the learning side, instead of training a narrow policy for every single task, you pretrain a large model on a broad mixture of data: real robot trajectories, simulation, human videos, and even the general world knowledge embedded in vision-language models. Then you fine-tune with a relatively small amount of task-specific data. That's the same pattern that worked so well for language, and we're starting to see it transfer.

The key piece, I think, is closing the loop with real-world data. Simulation is very valuable. It gives you scale, and it lets you explore dangerous or rare scenarios. But there's always a gap between simulation and reality: friction, deformable objects, sensor noise, unexpected human behavior. So the approach that makes the most sense to me is grounding learning in real-world experience and feeding deployment data back into training continuously. Every robot in the field becomes both a user of the model and a source of new data. That flywheel is exactly what we saw in autonomous driving. At Apollo, the vehicles on the road were constantly generating corner cases that improved the next version of the system.

On deployment, foundation models bring two big advantages. The first is generalization. Because the model has seen so much variety, it can handle new objects, new environments, and new instructions much more gracefully. The second is the interface. You can now instruct a robot in natural language, or show it a demonstration, rather than reprogramming it. That dramatically lowers the cost of putting robots into new settings, and cost of deployment has historically been the real barrier, more than raw capability.

That said, I want to be careful not to overstate where we are. There are still serious open problems. One is safety and reliability. In language, a 95% success rate is impressive. In the physical world, a 5% failure rate can mean broken equipment or someone getting hurt. Another is latency and compute. These models are large, and robots need to act in real time, often on the edge, with limited power. So a lot of work has to go into model compression, efficient inference, and the right split between on-device and cloud. A third is evaluation. We don't yet have benchmarks for embodied intelligence as mature as the ones we have for language.

So my view is that foundation models are the most promising path we've had for robotics in decades. They change the economics of both learning and deployment. But the winners will be the teams that combine strong models with real-world data loops, rigorous safety engineering, and very close collaboration between AI researchers and hardware people. This is where AI really meets the physical world, and I believe it's one of the most important frontiers for the next ten years.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think it gets at the heart of why I'm so excited about this moment in robotics.

Let me start with the problem. For decades, robotics has been stuck in what I'd call the "one robot, one task, one environment" paradigm. You build a robot arm for a factory, you program it for a specific assembly task, and it works beautifully, until you change the lighting, move the parts, or ask it to do something slightly different. Then it fails. The learning didn't generalize, and the deployment was brittle. Every new application essentially started from scratch. That's why robotics has lagged so far behind the digital world. Software scaled; robots didn't.

What foundation models bring is a fundamentally different approach. In language, we saw that if you train one very large model on enormous amounts of diverse data, it acquires general capabilities that transfer to tasks it was never explicitly trained for. The question for robotics has been: can we do the same thing for the physical world?

The R2R idea, what I think of broadly as real-to-real, is about closing that loop. Instead of learning in simulation and hoping it transfers, or collecting data from a single robot and hoping it generalizes, you build a foundation model that learns from real-world embodied experience across many robots, many embodiments, many environments, and then deploys back into the real world with continuous learning. The model becomes a shared "brain" that any physical body can plug into.

I see three concrete ways this addresses the learning problem.

First, data. Robotics has always been data-poor. You can't scrape the internet for robot trajectories the way you scrape it for text. But with a foundation model approach, every robot in deployment becomes a data collector. The fleet learns together. A failure in one warehouse in Shenzhen becomes a training signal that improves a robot in a hospital in Beijing. This is the flywheel we've never had before.

Second, cross-embodiment transfer. A foundation model trained on quadrupeds, humanoids, arms, and wheeled platforms learns something more abstract about physics, contact, and manipulation than any single-robot model could. We're seeing early evidence that skills learned on one body transfer, partially, to others. That dramatically reduces the cost of bringing up a new platform.

Third, the integration of language and vision with action. When the model already understands the world semantically, from pre-training on internet-scale vision and language, you can instruct a robot in natural language and it can reason about novel objects and situations. That's generalization, not memorization.

On the deployment side, the shift is equally important. Traditionally, deployment meant freezing the system. With a foundation model, deployment is where learning continues. The model can adapt to a specific site with a small amount of local data, the way we fine-tune a language model, while still inheriting the broad competence of the base model. And safety can be handled in layers: a fast low-level controller guaranteeing stability, with the foundation model providing high-level planning and adaptation above it.

Now, I want to be honest about the challenges, because I think there's a lot of hype right now. The data problem is not solved. We're still talking about millions of trajectories, not trillions of tokens. Physical actions have consequences, so you can't just let the model explore freely the way you can with text. Latency and compute on the edge are real constraints. And we don't yet have good benchmarks that tell us whether a robot foundation model is actually getting more general, rather than just memorizing more scenarios.

But the direction is clear. In my view, we're at the equivalent of the GPT-2 moment for embodied AI. The architecture is roughly right, the scaling trends are visible, and what remains is engineering, data, and time. In China especially, with the manufacturing base and the density of deployment scenarios, I think we're in a very strong position to accumulate the real-world data that drives this flywheel.

So to summarize: foundation models address learning by turning robotics from a data-poor, task-specific field into a data-rich, general one, and they address deployment by making it continuous and adaptive rather than frozen and brittle. It's the first time I've felt that the Moore's Law dynamic we had in computing could genuinely arrive in robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to connect learning with deployment. A robot needs to perceive its surroundings, reason about what to do, and then act in the physical world. Those capabilities have to work together, under conditions that are much less predictable than a purely digital environment.

Foundation models can give robots a shared starting point, so we don’t have to train every robot for every task from scratch. The challenge is turning that general knowledge into reliable physical behavior. Understanding an instruction is one thing; executing it with the right timing, force, and precision is another.

So I see R2R as a continuous learning loop: learn broadly, adapt to a particular robot and environment, and use experience from deployment to improve the model. Simulation can help us explore many situations, but real-world feedback is essential. The measure of success is whether we can reduce the amount of task-specific training while making deployment more reliable, adaptable, and safe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to connect learning with deployment much more closely. A robot has to perceive its environment, reason about what to do, and then act in the physical world. Those pieces have often been developed separately. Foundation models offer a way to bring them together and reuse what the robot has learned across different tasks.

But robotics has a very difficult data problem. Collecting real-world experience is expensive, and mistakes can damage equipment or hurt people. So we need a combination of demonstrations, simulation, and real-world interaction. The important question is whether that experience transfers: can a robot handle a new object, a different room, or a situation it has never encountered?

For deployment, the model also has to operate within practical constraints—latency, compute, power, and safety. I would expect a larger model to provide high-level reasoning, with more specialized models handling fast, precise control. Then deployment becomes part of the learning cycle: you identify failures, improve the model, validate it, and deploy again. That feedback loop is what can turn a foundation model into a useful robotic system.
